english: Let $S$ be the sphere $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-4x+2y-6z-86=0$ and let $\Pi$ be the plane $x+2y+2z+12=0$. The plane $\Pi$ cuts $S$ in a circle $\Gamma$. The line of intersection of $\Pi$ with the plane $2x+y-2z=15$ meets $\Gamma$ at the points $P$ and $Q$. Let $R$ be any point of the larger of the two arcs of $\Gamma$ determined by $P$ and $Q$. Then the value of $\cos\angle PRQ$ is ______.
hindi: माना कि $S$ गोला $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-4x+2y-6z-86=0$ है तथा $\Pi$ तल $x+2y+2z+12=0$ है। तल $\Pi$ गोले $S$ को एक वृत्त $\Gamma$ में काटता है। तल $\Pi$ तथा तल $2x+y-2z=15$ की प्रतिच्छेदन रेखा $\Gamma$ से बिन्दुओं $P$ तथा $Q$ पर मिलती है। माना कि $R$, $P$ तथा $Q$ द्वारा निर्धारित $\Gamma$ के दो चापों में से बड़े चाप का कोई बिन्दु है। तब $\cos\angle PRQ$ का मान ______ है।
solution: Normals $(1,2,2)\cdot(2,1,-2)=0$, so the second plane $\Sigma$ is perpendicular to $\Pi$; hence the distance of $F$ from the chord $PQ$ equals its distance from $\Sigma$: $\dfrac{|0-5+2-15|}{3}=6$
Perpendicular from the centre bisects $PQ$: half the central angle $\alpha=\frac12\angle PFQ$ has $\cos\alpha=\dfrac68=\dfrac34$
Inscribed angle on the major arc $=\frac12\angle PFQ=\alpha$, so $\cos\angle PRQ=\dfrac34=0.75$
solution_full: Distance of $C$ from $\Pi$: $\dfrac{|2-2+6+12|}{\sqrt{1+4+4}}=\dfrac{18}{3}=6<10$, so $\Gamma$ is a real circle of radius $\sqrt{100-36}=8$.
Its centre is the foot of the perpendicular from $C$: $F=C-\dfrac{18}{9}(1,2,2)=(0,-5,-1)$; check $0-10-2+12=0$.

Let $\Sigma$ be the plane $2x+y-2z=15$. Since $(1,2,2)\cdot(2,1,-2)=2+2-4=0$, $\Sigma\perp\Pi$. For a point $F$ of $\Pi$, the perpendicular from $F$ to $\Sigma$ then lies in $\Pi$ and meets $\Sigma$ on the line $\ell=\Pi\cap\Sigma$, so the distance of $F$ from $\ell$ equals its distance from $\Sigma$: $h=\dfrac{|0-5+2-15|}{3}=\dfrac{18}{3}=6$.

$h=6<8$, so $\ell$ cuts $\Gamma$ at two points $P$, $Q$. The perpendicular $FM$ from the centre to the chord bisects it, and in the right triangle $FMP$, $FM=6$, $FP=8$, so $\angle PFM=\alpha$ with $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{6}{8}=\dfrac34$ and $\angle PFQ=2\alpha$.

$\alpha<\frac{\pi}{2}$, so $\angle PFQ<\pi$ and the larger arc lies on the same side of $PQ$ as $F$. The angle subtended by a chord at a point of the major arc is half the angle at the centre, so $\angle PRQ=\alpha$ for every such $R$.
originality_note: New: a chord of a sphere's section circle is cut out by a second plane perpendicular to the section plane; the distance of the circle's centre from the chord comes from a point-plane distance, and the inscribed-angle theorem turns it into the angle at the circumference (way 5). Closest known: angle subtended by a chord at a point of the major arc of a given circle. Different because: the circle and the chord exist only as intersections in space, and the perpendicularity of the two planes is what makes the chord distance a plane distance.

concept_use.Sphere in three dimensions: Centre and radius of S, distance of the centre from Pi, foot of the perpendicular as the centre of the section circle, radius 8 = sqrt(100 - 36).
concept_use.Basic geometry about circle: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord (cos alpha = 6/8) and the angle at the circumference on the major arc is half the angle at the centre.

key_step: Finding the section circle (centre (0, -5, -1), radius 8) and the distance 6 of its centre from the chord, then the inscribed-angle theorem.
justification: Routine chain: sphere centre and radius, two point-plane distances, a perpendicular-plane observation and an inscribed-angle fact; no insight beyond noticing the planes are perpendicular. Like the conic-tangent chain of 2026-P2-Q17 (L2).
